facts.t: Sunscreen products, including aerosol sprays, have been recalled in the US, for example for benzene contamination.
Under FDA labeling rules, “Broad Spectrum” means the product passed a test for UVA protection in addition to UVB.
Sunscreens that are not Broad Spectrum, or are below SPF 15, must carry the warning: “This product has been shown only to help prevent sunburn, not skin cancer or early skin aging.”
FDA: choose a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 15.
The CDC: SPF 15 or higher, broad spectrum, every 2 hours.
The AAP: at least SPF 15 “(up to SPF 50)”; “an SPF of 15 or 30 should be fine for most people.”
The American Academy of Dermatology recommends SPF 30 or higher.
Health Canada recommends SPF 30 or higher.
FDA has proposed (not finalized) capping labeled SPF at 60+.

topics.title: Mineral or chemical UV filters

facts.t: The AAP's environmental health page says: “Mineral-based sunscreen (e.g., zinc oxide) is preferable to chemical-based sunscreen (e.g., oxybenzone).”
The AAP's 2021 safety tips say: “If possible, choose a sunscreen with the mineral ingredients zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.”
FDA has proposed (not finalized) that zinc oxide and titanium dioxide are generally recognized as safe and effective up to 25%.
For the 12 chemical filters, FDA has proposed that more safety data are needed.

In an FDA study in adults, six chemical filters (avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate, octinoxate) reached the blood above the level at which FDA asks for more safety testing, after one application.

other_side.t: FDA: “The fact that an ingredient is absorbed through the skin and into the body does not mean the ingredient is unsafe.”
FDA says its request for more data “does not represent a conclusion by the FDA” that those filters are unsafe.
The AAD says any of these sunscreens can protect you if it is broad spectrum, water resistant and SPF 30 or higher.
The AAP: “using any sunscreen is better than not using sunscreen at all.”

not_known: The absorption studies were done in adults; no study measured it in children.

facts.t: FDA: spray sunscreens “should never be applied directly to your face.”
The AAD advises never spraying around the face or mouth or into the wind, to avoid inhaling it.
A pediatric dermatologist writing on the AAP's site says spray propellants “should not be inhaled by babies and children.”
FDA lists aerosol sunscreens among products recalled for benzene contamination, a contaminant that never appears on a label.

other_side.t: The EU does not allow nano zinc oxide or nano titanium dioxide in uses that could expose the lungs, which in practice means sprays, so mineral sprays face the same caution.

facts.t: Every US sunscreen label says “children under 6 months: Ask a doctor.”
FDA: “Sunscreen is not recommended for infants under six months old”; the best protection is shade.
The AAP allows sunscreen on small areas such as the face if clothing and shade are not available.
Health Canada: “Do not put sunscreen on babies less than 6 months of age.”
“AAP does not recommend products that combine sunscreen with DEET.”
The AAD does not recommend sunscreen with insect repellent either.

other_side.t: Health Canada says sunscreen and insect repellents can be used safely together as separate products.

facts.t: FDA issued a final order in September 2026 that sunscreens with PABA or trolamine salicylate as actives are not generally recognized as safe and effective; it takes effect in September 2027.
FDA allows “Water Resistant (40 minutes)” or “(80 minutes)” only after a set water test.
FDA and the AAP advise reapplying at least every 2 hours, and after swimming, sweating or towel drying.
The AAP: “If possible, avoid the sunscreen ingredient oxybenzone because of concerns about mild hormonal properties.”
The EU limits oxybenzone to 6% in face, hand and lip products and 2.2% in body products and sprays.
Hawaii has banned the sale of sunscreens containing oxybenzone without a prescription since January 1, 2021.

other_side.t: FDA: absorption into the body “does not mean the ingredient is unsafe.”

facts.t: The EU allows homosalate only in face products (not propellant sprays), up to 7.34%.
That limit followed the EU scientific committee's opinion that homosalate is safe up to 7.34% in face cream and pump spray.
The US allows up to 15%.
Homosalate reached the blood above FDA's testing threshold in an FDA study in adults.

other_side.t: FDA says absorption does not mean an ingredient is unsafe, and has proposed only that more data are needed for homosalate.

topics.title: Octocrylene

facts.t: A 2021 study found benzophenone in all 15 octocrylene sunscreens tested, rising as the products aged.
California lists benzophenone under Proposition 65 as a chemical known to cause cancer.
EU law requires benzophenone from octocrylene to be kept at trace levels.
Australia's TGA recommended limiting benzophenone in sunscreens to 383 ppm.

other_side.t: The EU scientific committee found octocrylene safe as a UV filter up to 10%.

not_known: How much benzophenone a child's skin absorbs from an aged sunscreen has not been measured.

facts.t: Hawaii bans the sale of sunscreens containing oxybenzone or octinoxate without a prescription (Act 104, from January 1, 2021), citing harm to coral.
The AAP recommends SPF “at least 15 (up to SPF 50).”
FDA has proposed (not finalized) that the maximum labeled SPF be 60+.

topics.title: UV-absorbing ingredient listed as inactive

facts.t: Only the active ingredients in FDA's monograph may be used to make a sunscreen claim in the US.
This product lists {names} among its inactive ingredients.
Its maker sells butyloctyl salicylate as an SPF booster and says it is “responsible for no more than 2 SPF units” at 5%.
{status}
Butyloctyl and tridecyl salicylate are salicylates, the same chemical family as the filters homosalate and octisalate, which reached the blood above FDA's testing threshold in an FDA study in adults.
Vantage sells tridecyl salicylate as a “sunscreen booster” for zinc oxide and titanium dioxide.

not_known: No published study has measured whether butyloctyl salicylate or tridecyl salicylate is absorbed into the body.
How much of this product's SPF, if any, comes from these ingredients cannot be told from the label.

facts.t: The EU banned 4-methylbenzylidene camphor in cosmetics: none could be newly sold from May 1, 2025 and none at all from May 1, 2026.
The EU scientific committee could not set a safe concentration because possible genotoxicity could not be ruled out.

other_side.t: Australia still listed it as a permitted sunscreen filter (up to 4%) in its 2023 guidelines.

facts.t: FDA approved bemotrizinol as a sunscreen active ingredient (up to 6%), effective August 9, 2026.
Data submitted with the application showed it is not readily absorbed through human skin.
US rules let companies list all fragrance components as one word, “Fragrance”.
FDA says some fragrance components may cause allergic reactions or sensitivities.
For children with eczema, the AAD advises fragrance-free rather than “unscented” products and a fragrance-free sunscreen.
The EU requires named fragrance allergens to be listed individually above 0.001% in leave-on products.
The 2022 US law MoCRA required FDA to propose a similar fragrance allergen labeling rule by June 29, 2024.
As of FDA's July 2026 regulatory agenda, that proposal was scheduled for November 2026.

other_side.t: FDA says it does not have evidence that phthalates as used in cosmetics pose a safety risk.

topics.title: Lavender or tea tree oil

facts.t: A 2007 report described three healthy boys whose breast growth started while using lavender or tea tree oil products and stopped when the products were stopped.
NIEHS researchers found chemicals in these oils with estrogen-like or anti-androgen activity in cell tests; an NIEHS scientist described such effects in children as very rare.

not_known: Case reports cannot show the oils caused it; no safe or unsafe amount has been established.

facts.t: The EU has banned methylisothiazolinone in leave-on cosmetics since February 12, 2017, because no safe level for causing skin allergy was shown.
The EU requires products to be labeled “releases formaldehyde” when released formaldehyde exceeds 0.001%.
The EU bans propylparaben and butylparaben in leave-on products made for the diaper area of children under 3, because a risk for babies under 6 months could not be excluded.

other_side.t: The EU scientific committee found methylparaben and ethylparaben safe at permitted levels.

topics.title: Retinyl palmitate (vitamin A)

facts.t: In a 2012 government study, a cream with retinyl palmitate sped up skin tumors caused by simulated sunlight in hairless mice.
EU law adopted in 2024 caps vitamin A in body lotion at 0.05% and requires the label “Contains Vitamin A. Consider your daily intake before use.”

other_side.t: The EU scientific committee found vitamin A safe at those limits.

not_known: Whether the mouse finding applies to people has not been established; FDA has made no statement on it.

topics.title: Food-derived ingredients

facts.t: NIH peanut allergy guidelines single out infants with severe eczema, egg allergy, or both for early peanut introduction.
A UK study found peanut-oil creams used on babies' rashes were associated with a higher risk of peanut allergy.

not_known: The skin-exposure link comes from observational studies and is a hypothesis, not a proven cause. Refined oils may contain little protein; labels do not say.

topics.title: Citrus peel oil

facts.t: Furocoumarins, found naturally in some citrus oils, cause skin reactions in sunlight; EU law requires them to stay below 1 mg/kg in sun protection products.

not_known: The label does not say whether this oil has had its furocoumarins removed.

facts.t: The EU scientific committee found phenoxyethanol safe as a preservative up to 1%, including for young children.
France required a label against use on the diaper area of children under 3 in 2019; its highest administrative court annulled that decision in 2022 for lack of legal basis.

topics.title: PEG and other ethoxylated ingredients

facts.t: FDA says these ingredients can carry trace 1,4-dioxane, a manufacturing byproduct it calls a potential human carcinogen.
New York limits 1,4-dioxane to 10 ppm in cosmetics.

other_side.t: FDA reports the EU committee considered trace levels of 10 ppm or less safe, and that levels have fallen over time.

not_known: A label cannot show whether any 1,4-dioxane is present.

facts.t: The US National Toxicology Program lists BHA as reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen, based on animal studies.
California lists BHA under Proposition 65.

other_side.t: The EU scientific committee found BHT safe up to 0.8% in cosmetics.

facts.t: FDA says talc can be contaminated with asbestos, a known cause of cancer when inhaled.
FDA proposed asbestos testing of talc cosmetics in 2024 and withdrew the proposal in November 2025, saying it will issue a new one.
WHO's cancer agency classified talc as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A) in 2024.
Germany's BfR found no recognizable health risk from highly refined mineral oils on the skin.
The AAD recommends petroleum jelly for babies' diaper rash.

topics.title: Nano zinc oxide or titanium dioxide

facts.t: FDA wrote that zinc oxide stays mainly in the outer dead layers of the skin, whatever its particle size.
The EU allows nano zinc oxide and nano titanium dioxide up to 25%, but not in uses that could expose the lungs.
Australia's TGA concluded these nanoparticles are not likely to cause harm in sunscreens.
